planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring directly into humus-rich, consistently moist forest soil; this species rarely sets viable seed in cultivation, so vegetative propagation is the reliable method.

directions: Dwarf bramble is a low, trailing, nearly thornless Rubus of old-growth and mature second-growth conifer forests from southwestern British Columbia to northern California, spreading by slender runners that root at the nodes to form a loose evergreen groundcover under deep canopy. Small white flowers in late spring give way to sparse, soft red, few-drupelet berries that are pleasant but seldom abundant enough for more than a trailside nibble. It wants constant moisture, cool root conditions, and acidic, duff-rich soil, making it best suited to a shaded native woodland garden rather than a conventional fruiting bed. Because seed is rarely produced and slow to germinate, start new plantings from rooted sections of runner collected from an established patch.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
Pojar & MacKinnon, Plants of Coastal British Columbia

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil under open conifer or mixed-forest canopy; this species is adapted to cool, dappled-light understory conditions and resents hot, dry sites.

directions: Alaska blueberry is an understory shrub of coastal coniferous forests from southeast Alaska south through British Columbia to Oregon, where it forms loose colonies beneath hemlock and spruce canopy in deep, humus-rich duff. Pinkish, urn-shaped spring flowers are followed by small, dark blue, early-ripening berries with a mild, pleasant flavor similar to its close relative Vaccinium ovalifolium, with which it often hybridizes in the wild. It performs best with cool, consistently moist, acidic soil and benefits from the same mulching and pH management used for highbush blueberry, but needs considerably more shade to thrive. Because it is rarely offered by mainstream nurseries, source container stock from native-plant specialists in the Pacific Northwest.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
E-Flora BC Atlas of the Plants of British Columbia

planting.note: Plant rooted runner sections in spring in cool, acidic, humus-rich soil under conifer canopy; snow bramble trails along the forest floor and roots as it spreads, so division of an existing patch is far more reliable than seed.

directions: Snow bramble is a prostrate, glossy-leaved, nearly thornless evergreen Rubus native to coniferous forests from British Columbia to northern California and the inland Rockies, where it carpets shaded, duff-covered ground alongside sword fern and salal. Small white flowers in spring produce a scattering of bright red, thimble-sized berries with a pleasant, mild raspberry flavor, prized more for their appearance against the glossy foliage than for any real harvest. It needs the same cool, consistently moist, acidic woodland conditions as its relatives and makes an attractive, low-maintenance evergreen groundcover for a shaded native planting once established. Propagate by lifting and replanting rooted sections of the trailing stems rather than relying on seed, which germinates slowly and unevenly.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
Pojar & MacKinnon, Plants of Coastal British Columbia

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist to wet, strongly acidic, sandy peat soil in partial shade to full sun; this species is adapted to the boggy, nutrient-poor conditions of Atlantic coastal plain bogs and pine barrens.

directions: New Jersey blueberry is a highbush-type species native to acidic bogs, cedar swamp margins, and pine-barren wetlands of the Atlantic coastal plain from New England to the Carolinas, where it grows in standing or seasonally saturated water that would rot the roots of upland blueberry species. Urn-shaped spring flowers give way to sweet, dark blue summer berries closely resembling cultivated highbush blueberry, to which it is a close wild relative. It thrives in the dappled shade at a bog or swamp margin and should be planted in constantly moist, sandy peat with no lime amendment, mirroring the nutrient-poor, saturated soils of its pine-barren habitat. Because it tolerates wetter ground and somewhat more shade than most blueberry cultivars, it is a useful choice for the shaded, boggy edge of a native rain garden where standard blueberries struggle.

planting.note: Plant root divisions or sucker clumps in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge or thicket margin; this bramble tolerates more shade than most blackberries but fruits best with at least a few hours of direct sun.

directions: Bristly blackberry is a low, densely bristled, thicket-forming native bramble of the Great Lakes region and northeastern North America, found naturally along moist woodland margins, fencerows, and the partly shaded edges of bogs and thickets. Its stems bear fine, needle-like bristles rather than true thorns, and the small, tart, dark berries ripen in mid to late summer, more useful for jam and wildlife forage than fresh eating. It spreads readily by root suckers to form a low tangled thicket, making it a good choice for stabilizing a shaded, moist slope or naturalizing a woodland-edge hedgerow rather than a formal berry row. Thin out old, spent canes each year after fruiting to keep the thicket productive and prevent it from becoming overly congested.
